Are there brave children here? The celebration of Sinterklaas through the ages

Picture of Sinterklaas

As most of you know, Santa Claus is derived from the Dutch figure of Sinterklaas. As the season is coming up I have decided to write a little bit about Sinterklaas and a theory of his history linking all the way back to the Viking Age and the uses of the Germanic tribes!

During the Viking-age

The etymology of Nicolaas is from the word Hnikkar, one of the many names of Odin. It roughly translates to “the one who takes the dead”. The word Harii, the black army of Nicolaas, is etymologically connected to –herjar, as in “einherjar”, the wild hunt… so Nicolaas and his black helpers were depicting Odin and the army of living dead of the wild hunt. Tacitus has also written about this practice within Germanic tribes: painting oneself black before battle to pledge oneself to Odin and prepare to become part of his living dead army.

Santa Claus is very concerned about “naughty” children, as is Sinterklaas today. He always asks: “are there naughty [stoute] children here? Those who aren’t naughty get hands full of candy and even presents. But a big difference between Santa and Sinterklaas is the coal-giving. The children who are naughty will be put in a huge sack and taken by Sinterklaas. Nowadays it’s a great story to scare children into behaving, but the Dutch word “stout” only has the connotation of “naughty” for a very short while. It used to mean “brave”. Nicolaas would come into your home with his army of figures that are completely black of soot and would ask: are there brave children here? The children who didn’t dare to go with him would get candy, but those who turned old and brave would eventually rise up to the challenge and say: yes, I am! The child would be taken into the bag and out the door, then when he was taken out of the bag it was revealed that the person dressing as Nicolaas was actually the oldest male relative and all the others were brothers, cousins etc. Then the child would get painted black with soot and become one of the helpers of Nicolaas, the harii. It was a huge part of the coming-of-age process of a child, he conquered his fears and is now an adult. He is the one tricking the children from now on as one of the Harii serving Nicolaas and looking for other brave children. This entire tradtion is rooted in being brave, conquering your fear, but also trickery... sounds like Odin to me!

Dark Ages:

When Christianity took over they also took over the festivities of December 5th. In the Christian mythos there are many legends that go back to their Saint Nicolaas van Myra, but without details around what time this legendary figure supposed to have lived. One of the curious things is that this Sinterklaas has a black beast with horns, who was his helper and who is cuffed in chains. His name? Ruprecht. One of the names of Odin. Black Pete was a demon, chained and subdued by Saint Nicholas who was his master. This is the Christian influence in the celebration, putting the emphasis on the contrast between good and evil. By placing a pagan god in the submission of a Christian saint, the dominance of Christianity grew. Besides that, Odin is depicted as a black beast, like the devil. A nickname for the Devil in that time was Old Nic. Is this a reference to the Old Nicolaas? Another name for Ruprecht (Odin) became Zwarte Piet (black pete), which was also a name for the devil. Yes, Christianity, we get it: you really don’t like Odin, do you? Click here for a picture of Ruprecht, or Grampus

Golden Age and Controversy:

We leave the middle ages with Zware Piet as a hairy beast with hooves and horns. But during the Golden Ages the appearance of him changes to a stereotypical blackface. The first documentations of Zwarte Piet being black and having afro-like hair are from the 19th century. From 1815 the Dutch Republic had several colonies up until the Second World War. These colonies include Brazil, India, South Afrika, Sri Lanka, Ghana, Niger, Surinam and some more. There is a theory in Cultural Theory and Popular Culture that racism first began as a defensive ideology to defend the profits from the slave trade. If this ideology was generally accepted, then it would be a completely acceptable situation to gain profit over the lives of others. Christianity used the image of Black Pete and Saint Nicholas to gain power, to show that there is a natural relationship of submission between the Christian and Pagan god. It would only fit the ideology of race to show this natural relationship of submission between black people and the white saint.

Two centruries before all this, in 1626 the Dutch settle in New Netherlands and build a little place called New Amsterdam, which after trading off this colony for Surinam with England get's renamed to New York. The Dutch settelers have already brought the tradition of Sinterklaas with them and apparently the English didn't root out this tradition but butchered up the name to Santa Claus. This is the main reason why the helpers of Sinterklaas and Santa Claus look so different, this was two centuries before someone thought of the idea to depict Zwarte Piet as a blackface.

Contemporary celebration:

Nicolaas still rides on his horse over the rooftops of the houses, just as Odin rides through the sky on Sleipnir. Therefore, it is still custom to put your shoes by the fireplace during the weeks running up to Sinterklaas evening and leave a carrot for the horse in the shoe. This goes back centuries, as also beeing described by Tacitus: during the winter Germanic tribes would leave offerings by the hearth inside of their shoes and socks, mainly carrots and hay for Sleipnir.

Nicolaas and his helpers still threaten to take you in a bag if you’ve been bad, and give out candy and presents to those who have been good.

The looks of Zwarte Piet has been a point of discussion for many years, as most countries besides the Netherlands think the entire celebration of a white man with a bunch of black slaves is blatantly racist and not done. Click for picture and see for yourself, especially notice all the bags they are holding and their black-made skin colour A lot of people want the character of Zwarte Piet to be banished forever or perhaps even the entire celebration. Some want the character of Zware Piet to get changed back to the black and hairy beast of Ruprecht. The discussion is never ending.

Bare in mind, just like with all research, that there are a lot of different sources for the mythological figure of Sinterklaas, this is one of the plausible theories. We ofcourse can’t exactly reconstruct the celebration in the Viking age but this is one of the most leading theories that has been based on different sources and research.
